Conjecture
kŏn-jĕk´chūr
n. (a guess; an opinion formed on evidence that does not amount to proof)
Latin conjicere, to throw together, from con- and jacere, to cast. A conjecture is a throwing-together of what is known in the hope of reaching what is not.

Biblical Definition

Conjecture is opinion beyond the evidence, and Scripture draws a boundary around it. The line is stated once for all: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deu 29:29). The Lord forbids a particular conjecture: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power” (Act 1:7). Judgment of persons is reserved: “judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come” (1Co 4:5). God's answer to Job is a series of questions: “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4). And Paul ends his hardest argument in doxology: “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines conjecture as an opinion or judgment formed on defective or presumptive evidence; a supposition; a guess; a surmise.

expand to see more

CONJECTURE, n. Literally, a casting or throwing together of possible or probable events; or a casting together of circumstances.

Hence, an opinion or judgment formed on defective or presumptive evidence; probable inference; surmise; guess.

CONJECTURE, v.t. To guess; to judge by guess, or by the probability or the possibility of a fact, or by very slight evidence.

Key Scripture

Deu 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

Act 1:7 — "And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power."

1Co 4:5 — "Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God."

Job 38:4 — "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding."

Rom 11:33 — "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!"

Modern Corruption

Conjecture is preached with the confidence of revelation, and Deuteronomy assigns the secret things elsewhere.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 29:29 is the most useful verse in the Bible for a theologian and its structure is a division of property. The secret things belong unto the LORD our God; the revealed things belong unto us and to our children for ever — and the purpose clause governs both: that we may do all the words of this law. What is revealed is given for obedience rather than for speculation, and what is not revealed is not ours to reconstruct. A great deal of confident preaching about the unrevealed is trespass, and a great deal of comfortable ignorance about the revealed is theft.

Acts 1:7 is the Lord's reply to the last question the apostles ever asked Him, and it is a rebuke wrapped in a commission. They ask whether He will at this time restore the kingdom to Israel; He says it is not for you to know the times or the seasons — and then immediately, but ye shall receive power… and ye shall be witnesses unto me. The energy that would have gone into chronology is redirected into mission. Every generation's date-setting has ignored a verse spoken directly to the question, by the One who would know.

The other misuse is conjecture about people, and it is commoner in congregations than conjecture about prophecy. First Corinthians 4:5 forbids judging before the time until the Lord come, who… will make manifest the counsels of the hearts — and motives are precisely what no one can see. A church can and must judge conduct, which is visible; it cannot judge the heart behind it, and the confident attribution of motive is the most damaging conjecture ordinary Christians engage in. Romans 11:33 is where the honest theologian ends, and it is not a defeat: the doxology comes after eleven chapters of the hardest argument in Scripture, not instead of them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nistaroth (H5641), the secret things; niglath (H1540), the things revealed; Greek chronoi kai kairoi (G5550, G2540), times and seasons; anexereunetos (G419), unsearchable.

expand to see more

Hebrew hannistaroth / hanniglot (H5641, H1540) — the secret things / the revealed things; Deuteronomy 29:29.

Greek chronous e kairous (G5550, G2540) — times or seasons; Acts 1:7, 1 Thessalonians 5:1.

Greek anexereunetos / anexichniastos (G419, G421) — unsearchable, past finding out; Romans 11:33.

Usage

"“The secret things belong unto the LORD our God” — a division of property."

"“It is not for you to know the times” — then, but ye shall be witnesses."

"“The counsels of the hearts” — which is exactly what no one can see."
